rationale: Hand-curated cross-reference graph for the 35-doc RAG corpus. When a doc is retrieved as primary evidence, related docs surface as 'see also' entries — gives the model an opening to cite the supplementing protocol, the controlling national statute, or the operational manual it would otherwise miss. Kept small (~30 edges) and human-curated rather than auto-extracted because legal cross-references are subtle (e.g., 'amended by' vs 'supersedes for jurisdiction X' carry different weight). Schema is intentionally simple: from/to are RAG_CORPUS ids, relation is a free-form short verb phrase, note is the human-readable why.

relations_glossary.supplemented_by: Later instrument that adds obligations without replacing the earlier one (e.g., a Protocol to a Convention).
relations_glossary.operationalized_by: Later document that turns a high-level obligation into measurable indicators or procedures.
relations_glossary.supersedes_for_corridor: Replaces an earlier instrument's effect for a specific migration corridor / use case.
relations_glossary.derives_authority_from: Implementing regulation that draws statutory authority from a parent act.
relations_glossary.mirrors: Different jurisdiction enacts the same substantive rule.
relations_glossary.same_convention: Two corpus entries are different articles or excerpts of the same convention.
relations_glossary.complements: Different statutes that get cited together because they cover adjacent aspects of the same fact pattern.
relations_glossary.complementary_framework: Different international frameworks that apply jointly to the same case (e.g., forced labour AND trafficking).
relations_glossary.sister_protocol: Two protocols that together complete a treaty package.
relations_glossary.applied_in_jurisdiction: International convention's domestic-law expression in a specific state.
relations_glossary.sectoral_application: Convention applied to a specific sector or worker category.
relations_glossary.evidence_for: NGO/research brief providing field evidence for a statutory framework.
relations_glossary.references_indicator: Convention article that incorporates a specific ILO Forced Labour Indicator by reference.
relations_glossary.cross_referenced_in_remittance_flows: AML / cross-border financial flow analysis that intersects with the trafficking framework.

edges.note: P029 (2014) adds State obligations on victim identification, remedies, and recruitment regulation that C029 (1930) lacked.
The 11 indicators turn C029's abstract definition into a field-usable checklist.
Document retention (Art. 9 of C189) is exactly Indicator 7 of the C029 operational manual.
Both excerpts are from C181; the second restates the no-fees rule with sector-applicability emphasis.
MC 14-2017 explicitly governs the PH-HK domestic-worker corridor; MC 02-2007 still applies to other zero-fee destinations.
POEA MC 14-2017 is implementing regulation; statutory base is RA 8042 / RA 10022.
Same statutory base — both circulars apply RA 8042's prohibition on excess fees.
Nepal's free-visa-free-ticket rule is the domestic expression of the C181 'no fees from workers' principle.
BP2MI's allocation of recruitment costs to the employer parallels C181's ban on worker-paid fees.
HK Employment Ord. + EA Reg. 57A together govern HK-side recruitment + agency fee caps for FDH cases.
Debt bondage cases require BOTH: Money Lenders Ord. for the loan vehicle, Employment Ord. for the wage-deduction analysis.
HK's commission cap operationalizes the C189 protections for domestic workers in HK jurisdiction.
Singapore EFMA §22A is SG's analog of HK's EA Reg. 57A for foreign domestic workers.
C188 applies forced-labour-prevention obligations to the fishing sector specifically.
Cross-border value transfers tied to recruitment fees fall under both anti-trafficking and AML frameworks.
The two Palermo Protocols (Trafficking + Smuggling-of-Migrants) form a single Convention package.
ILO Forced-Labour and Palermo Trafficking apply jointly to the same case; ILO is broader (any work), Palermo requires acquisition by deception/coercion for exploitation.
P029 fills victim-remedy gaps that the older trafficking framework left to discretion.
IJM 2023 brief documents debt bondage cases against the 11 indicators — useful for case validation.
Polaris 2024 typology maps recruitment-fraud schemes seen in PH outbound corridors.
Two articles of C095 (wage protection); together they govern wage deductions for employment.
C095 Art. 9's prohibition on deductions to obtain employment is operationalized in HK's lender regulations when the lender is the recruitment counterparty.
HK Employment Ord. §32 is the domestic-law route for enforcing C189 Art. 9 document-retention protections.
RA 8042 §6(j) (illegal recruitment by retention of travel documents) is the PH-side enforcement path for C189 Art. 9 protections.
The complaint-procedure entry walks through how to invoke RA 8042's prohibitions in practice.
Same procedural path applies whether the complaint cites the MC or the underlying RA.
C143 (1975) supplements C097 (1949) by explicitly extending equal-treatment rights to undocumented migrants for past-employment claims.
C143 sets the general migrant-worker non-discrimination floor; C189 Art. 9 applies it specifically to domestic workers.
C190 (2019) adds the violence + harassment framework on top of C189's domestic-worker protections; together they cover sexual violence + retaliation in employer-provided accommodation.
C190 (gender-based + economic harm in the world of work) and CEDAW GR 38 (trafficking as gender-based violence) jointly frame the structural-violence analysis.
WHO Global Code Art. 3.5 prohibits worker-paid recruitment fees in health-personnel context — sector-specific expression of C181 Art. 7's universal no-fees rule.
Healthcare sector (nurses, caregivers) often overlaps with domestic-work protections; both apply jointly when a nurse is also residing in employer-provided accommodation.
EU 2024 amendment translates Palermo definitions into binding EU member-state law with online-platform risk-assessment obligations.
EU Directive (binding on EU member states) + Council of Europe Convention 197 (broader 47-state framework) jointly cover the European trafficking-victim-protection space.
ACTIP is the ASEAN regional implementation of Palermo, with operational mutual-legal-assistance + extradition provisions tuned to Southeast Asian cross-border cases.
ACTIP is the binding treaty; Bali Process is the operational coordination framework. Together they govern Southeast Asian cross-border trafficking cooperation.
CoE Convention 197 is Council of Europe's regional implementation of Palermo, with stronger victim-rights guarantees (30-day reflection period, residence permit independent of cooperation).
CEDAW GR 38 frames trafficking as gender-based violence under CEDAW Art. 6, providing a state-reporting mechanism that complements Palermo's criminal-justice framework.
UNCRC Art. 35 is child-specific trafficking protection; Palermo Art. 3(c) (children cannot consent) is the operational rule for trafficking cases involving minors.
UNCRC + ILO C138 (Minimum Age, 1973) + C182 (Worst Forms of Child Labour, 1999) together form the child-labour framework on top of C029's general forced-labour prohibition.
Climate-mobility framework recognises climate-displaced workers as needing the C097 migration-employment baseline; bilateral agreements (RSE / PALM / PALM+) are the implementation.
Bali Process operationalizes ACTIP cooperation via the Working Group on Trafficking in Persons + Regional Support Office for cross-border investigation coordination.
C188 + C190 jointly cover fishing-vessel forced-labour cases that combine isolation + sectoral abuse + violence patterns.
FATF Recommendation 32 (cross-border cash) intersects with C097's protections when wages are routed through opaque financial channels rather than the worker's own bank account.

ILO Indicator 5 (physical and sexual violence) overlaps with C190's broader violence-and-harassment framework — C190 covers cases that don't meet the criminal-violence threshold but still constitute world-of-work violence.

CEDAW GR 38 explicitly identifies kafala-system structural reform as a state obligation under CEDAW Art. 6; combined with C189 Art. 9's domestic-worker protections this is the structural-reform argument.
